about.title: About Me
about.content: I am an Assistant Professor of Astrostatistics at the University of Toronto, jointly appointed between the David A. Dunlap Department of Astronomy & Astrophysics and the Department of Statistical Sciences. I am also an Associate Member of the Dunlap Institute for Astronomy & Astrophysics and a Member of the Data Sciences Institute, and I co-lead the interdisciplinary Astrostatistics Research Team (ART) alongside Gwen Eadie.
paragraphs: I am an Assistant Professor of Astrostatistics jointly appointed between the David A. Dunlap Department of Astronomy & Astrophysics and the Department of Statistical Sciences at the University of Toronto. I am also an Associate Member of the Dunlap Institute for Astronomy & Astrophysics as well as a Member of the Data Sciences Institute. For the 2026–2027 academic year, I am also serving as the (Interim) Director of the MScAC – Data Science Concentration in the Department of Statistical Sciences.

My research lies at the intersection of astrostatistics, data science, and artificial intelligence. Together with the Astrostatistics Research Team (ART), which I co-lead with Gwen Eadie, I develop and apply statistical and machine-learning methods to large datasets to answer complex astrophysical questions and improve how we learn about the universe from noisy, messy data.

I also teach undergraduate and graduate courses in astronomy and statistics, serve on committees within the University of Toronto, and remain active in professional societies including the AAS, ASA-AIG, SSC-DSA, and CASCA. I also help manage the Astronomy & Astrophysics Summer Undergraduate Research Program (SURP), the largest program of its kind in Canada.

team.title: The Astrostatistics Research Team (ART)

logo.alt: Astrostatistics Research Team Logo - A stylized constellation forming the letters ART

team.content: I co-lead the interdisciplinary Astrostatistics Research Team (ART) at the University of Toronto with its founder, Gwen Eadie. Our group brings together faculty, postdoctoral fellows, graduate students, and undergraduate researchers across Astronomy & Astrophysics, Statistical Sciences, Computer Science, and the Dunlap Institute to work on shared methodological, AI, and astrophysical problems.

highlights.title: Statistical Methodology, AI & Open Software
highlights.content: We develop Bayesian sampling algorithms, simulation-based inference methods, and scientific AI foundation models, releasing open-source packages and data products built directly around questions in observational and theoretical astrophysics.

highlights.title: Cross-Departmental Community
highlights.content: Our group spans Astronomy & Astrophysics, Statistical Sciences, and the Dunlap Institute, with weekly group meetings, reading groups, hack days, and joint co-supervision.

areas.title: Statistical Learning & AI
areas.description: Building multimodal foundation models, normalizing flows, and AI/LLM systems to uncover structure across massive, noisy, heterogeneous astronomical surveys.

areas.title: Interpretability & Insight
areas.description: Investigating the mathematical and statistical foundations of deep learning and representation spaces so we can calibrate uncertainty and trust scientific conclusions drawn from AI models.

areas.title: Inference & Computation
areas.description: Designing dynamic nested sampling, Markov chain Monte Carlo, and simulation-based inference algorithms that make rigorous Bayesian inference and model comparison tractable at survey scale.

areas.title: Discovery & Understanding
areas.description: Applying these frameworks to billion-star photometric, astrometric, and spectroscopic surveys to map the Milky Way in 3-D and trace how stars, star clusters, dust, and galaxies form and evolve.

collaboration.title: Working With Me
collaboration.intro: Collaboration and mentorship are central to how I do research. Whether you are a prospective postdoctoral fellow, graduate student, undergraduate researcher, or visiting collaborator, here are the core values of our group and the primary pathways for joining.

items.title: Equity, Diversity, and Inclusion
items.content: For centuries, explicit and implicit discrimination have barred individuals from many backgrounds from participating fully and freely in science. As scientists and people, we have a duty to address these injustices to better both our profession and society at large. I endeavor to create a community in which all members feel that their diverse backgrounds can be an integral part of their identity as a scientist rather than something that excludes them from being a valued member of the scientific community.

items.title: Open and Accessible Science
items.content: I am a strong proponent of open, accessible, and reproducible science. When conducting research, my collaborators and I make an active effort to share our results along with public data products, interactive visualizations, and open-source code that remains public throughout its development and well-documented when released to the wider community.

cards.title: Postdoctoral Researchers
cards.content: Gwen Eadie and I are always glad to hear from prospective postdocs interested in joining the Astrostatistics Research Team. Because openings depend on funding, most postdoctoral fellows join through one of the fellowships below. If one matches your timeline and research interests, please email either of us well before the application deadline.

cards.title: Graduate Students
cards.content: Faculty at the University of Toronto do not admit graduate students directly; admissions are handled by our departmental committees. The first step is applying to one of the Master's or PhD programs below. If you are interested in working together, feel free to email me before you apply to discuss potential projects.

cards.title: University of Toronto Undergraduates
cards.content: I work with University of Toronto undergraduates both during the academic year and over the summer. To keep applications and review equitable, I advertise most undergraduate projects through the university programs below.

cards.title: Canadian Undergraduates
cards.content: Students at other Canadian universities typically join our group for paid summer research terms through one of the competitive summer fellowships below.

cards.title: International Undergraduates
cards.content: Several funded exchange programs support international undergraduates for summer or semester research terms at Canadian universities. Eligibility depends on your home institution and country, so please check the program details below before applying.

cards.title: Visiting Researchers & External Collaborators
cards.content: I welcome new collaborations as well as short- or long-term research visits to the University of Toronto. If you are interested in visiting or collaborating on a project, please reach out by email at j.speagle@utoronto.ca so we can discuss scope and funding.

narrative: I spent much of my childhood moving between the United States (around Milwaukee and Brookfield, Wisconsin) and China (Beijing and Shanghai). I fell in love with astronomy and physics at age 17 after reading From Eternity to Here by Sean Carroll, which led me to Harvard University, where I completed my Bachelor’s Degree with Honors in Astrophysics and Physics in 2015.

Working across several undergraduate research projects at Harvard highlighted how deeply modern science relies on statistical analysis and computation, shifting my focus toward astrostatistics and data science. I spent 2015–2016 in Kashiwa, Japan with Alexie Leauthaud and Kevin Bundy at the Kavli Institute for the Physics and Mathematics of the Universe (Kavli IPMU) working on photometric redshifts for the Hyper Suprime-Cam survey, before returning to Harvard to complete my Master’s and PhD in Astronomy (2020) on “Mapping the Milky Way in the Age of Gaia” under Doug Finkbeiner, Charlie Conroy, Alyssa Goodman, and Daniel Eisenstein.

In 2020, I moved to the University of Toronto as a Banting and Dunlap Postdoctoral Fellow working with Gwen Eadie. In 2022, I joined her on the faculty as an Assistant Professor in Astrostatistics jointly appointed between the David A. Dunlap Department of Astronomy & Astrophysics and the Department of Statistical Sciences, where we co-lead the Astrostatistics Research Team (ART).

biography.personalNote: Outside of work, I mostly enjoy hanging out at home or going out with my wife, our two dogs, and our son. I also watch way too much anime, play way too many video games, and have a supremely unhealthy love of junk food and soda.

philosophy.title: Teaching Philosophy
philosophy.content: I am passionate about education and pedagogy, with a focus on practical skills such as programming, applied statistics, and data analysis that are not often taught as part of a traditional science curriculum. To foster student engagement, I focus on teaching methods built around a “flipped classroom” setting where students discuss and complete interactive exercises with peers, providing a framework for frequent, “low-risk” participation, encouraging peer collaboration, and lowering barriers to asking questions. There is a clear connection between mental health and academic success, and as an instructor my responsibility is to foster an environment where students can achieve both by building relationships grounded in empathy and kindness.

pillars.title: Conceptual Mastery
pillars.content: Students should gain a deep understanding of the underlying themes and concepts of the course. This enables students to build intuition as well as transfer skills and knowledge gained from the course to other areas throughout their careers.

pillars.title: Experiential Learning
pillars.content: The most effective ways to learn always involve “hands-on” experience. Students should have numerous opportunities to directly apply the knowledge and skills they are learning to relevant problems, discuss these experiences with their peers, and pursue long-term projects with substantial autonomy over their focus and execution.

pillars.title: Accessibility, Equity & Inclusion
pillars.content: Students should have the ability to access, pursue, and learn from these opportunities regardless of their background. Courses should be explicitly designed to reward diverse backgrounds so students feel their unique identities strengthen their connection to the material and sense of belonging in the scientific community.

items.title: Five new postdoctoral fellows and PhD students join our group at U of T
items.blurb: Postdoctoral fellows Christian Kragh Jespersen (Schmidt AI in Science & CITA National Fellow), Maryum Sayeed (Arts & Science Fellow), and Chloe Cheng (Research Excellence Fellow), along with doctoral students Ian Zhang and Isabelle Huang, join our research group at the University of Toronto.

items.title: Mairead Heiger completes her PhD, joins UVA as a joint GECO/CosmicAI postdoctoral fellow
items.blurb: Mairead Heiger successfully defended her PhD in the David A. Dunlap Department of Astronomy & Astrophysics (co-supervised with Ting Li) and joins the University of Virginia as a joint GECO and CosmicAI Postdoctoral Fellow.

items.title: Mairead Heiger and Simran Nerval win the 2026 Fieldus Award
items.blurb: Mairead Heiger and Simran Nerval received the department’s Fieldus Award recognizing a high level of research acumen and service. Mairead was honored for her spectroscopic follow-up of the ultra-faint dwarf galaxies Eridanus IV and Centaurus I, her galactic chemical evolution modeling framework, and her leadership as GASA co-chair.

items.title: Constraining supernova yields and delay times from dwarf spheroidal galaxies
items.blurb: Led by PhD student Mairead Heiger (with Ting Li and collaborators), our new study uses Bayesian chemical evolution modeling of Milky Way dwarf spheroidal galaxies to constrain Type Ia and core-collapse supernova nucleosynthetic yields and delay-time distributions.

items.title: A deep 3-D dust map of the southern Galactic plane from DECaPS2
items.blurb: Co-led with Catherine Zucker and Andrew Saydjari (ApJ, 992, 39), we inferred distances and extinctions for over 550 million stars in the DECaPS2 survey using brutus to construct the deepest 3-D dust map of the southern Milky Way plane.

items.title: Steffani Grondin and Michael Poon win the 2025 Jui Lin (Allen) Yen Award
items.blurb: Steffani Grondin and Michael Poon received the department’s Jui Lin (Allen) Yen Award for exceptional graduate research achievement, recognizing Steffani’s doctoral thesis on white dwarf binaries, extra-tidal stars, and dynamical ejections in star clusters.

items.title: Steffani Grondin completes her PhD, joins UC San Diego as an NSERC postdoctoral fellow
items.blurb: Steffani Grondin successfully defended her PhD in Astronomy & Astrophysics (co-supervised with Maria Drout and Jeremy Webb) and joins UC San Diego as an NSERC Postdoctoral Fellow.

items.title: Sam Berek completes her PhD, joins UMass Amherst as an NSF postdoctoral fellow
items.blurb: Sam Berek successfully defended her PhD in the David A. Dunlap Department of Astronomy & Astrophysics (co-supervised with Gwen Eadie) and joins UMass Amherst as an NSF Astronomy and Astrophysics Postdoctoral Fellow.

items.title: ChronoFlow: an AI model for the ages of stars
items.blurb: Led by PhD student Phil Van-Lane (co-supervised with Gwen Eadie; ApJ, 987, 152), ChronoFlow uses conditional normalizing flows calibrated on open star clusters to infer stellar rotation-age posteriors across the Milky Way, with press coverage in U of T News and Phys.org.

items.title: First white dwarf–main-sequence binary candidates in open star clusters
items.blurb: Led by PhD student Steffani Grondin (ApJ, 976, 207), our team combined Gaia DR3, GALEX ultraviolet photometry, and machine learning to identify 52 post-common-envelope white dwarf–main-sequence binary candidates across 38 open star clusters, covered by U of T Arts & Science, Phys.org, and SciTechDaily.

items.title: Sam Berek and Shivan Khullar win the 2024 Jui Lin (Allen) Yen Award
items.blurb: Sam Berek and Shivan Khullar received the department’s Jui Lin (Allen) Yen Award. Sam was honored for her paper introducing zero-inflated Bayesian hierarchical count models (HERBAL) to model galaxy–globular cluster scaling relations.

items.title: A 5-D map of the Milky Way: AAS Nova featured image
items.blurb: Our lead-author study (Speagle et al. 2024, ApJ, 971, 136) mapping distances, extinctions, and stellar properties for 170 million stars across the Milky Way using brutus was highlighted as an AAS Nova Featured Image.

items.title: Students train AI for the Galaxy Zoo: Euclid citizen-science project
items.blurb: U of T Statistical Sciences profiled undergraduate researchers Khalid Edris and Junbo (Felix) Li, co-mentored with Dunlap Fellow Mike Walmsley, on fine-tuning the Zoobot foundation model to classify galaxy morphologies from the Euclid space telescope.

items.title: Connaught New Researcher Award
items.blurb: Awarded the University of Toronto’s Connaught New Researcher Award in support of early-career faculty research in astrostatistics, Bayesian inference, and survey science.

items.title: DECaPS2: a survey of 3.3 billion objects in the Milky Way's plane
items.blurb: The second data release of the Dark Energy Camera Plane Survey (Saydjari et al. 2023, ApJS, 264, 28) catalogued 3.32 billion objects across 6.5% of the night sky in the southern Galactic plane, with press coverage in NSF NOIRLab, Space.com, PBS NewsHour, and Salon.

items.title: 2022 John Charles Polanyi Prize in Physics
items.blurb: Awarded the 2022 John Charles Polanyi Prize in Physics by the Council of Ontario Universities and the Government of Ontario in recognition of early-career research in statistical astronomy and Milky Way cartography.

items.title: The Local Bubble: the Sun sits in a 1,000-light-year void that forms stars
items.blurb: Using 3-D dust maps and Gaia space astrometry, our Nature study (Zucker et al. 2022) showed that virtually all nearby young star-forming complexes lie on the expanding surface of the Local Bubble, covered by CfA, the Harvard Gazette, STScI, and Smithsonian Magazine.

items.title: Mapping the Milky Way: an interactive tool for 170 million stars
items.blurb: Profiled by the Dunlap Institute for Astronomy & Astrophysics on developing the allsky interactive panchromatic sky visualization and mapping 170 million stars and interstellar dust across the Galaxy.

items.title: dynesty published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
items.blurb: The release paper for dynesty, our open-source Python package for dynamic nested sampling and Bayesian posterior and evidence estimation, appeared in MNRAS (493, 3132) and has now been cited over 2,200 times.

items.title: The Radcliffe Wave: the largest gaseous structure in the galaxy
items.blurb: Co-authored the Nature discovery (Alves et al. 2020) of a coherent 9,000-light-year undulation of interconnected star-forming clouds in the solar neighborhood using 3-D dust mapping with brutus, featured by CfA and the Harvard Gazette.
